opus-5.5.text:
I think the landscape is splitting in a fairly natural way. The big labs — OpenAI, Google, Anthropic — have an enormous advantage in compute, data pipelines, and engineering infrastructure, so the frontier of pretraining at scale is really their game. If a small company tries to compete head-on by training a bigger general-purpose model, that's usually a losing strategy, because the gap in resources compounds over time.

But that doesn't mean small companies have no room. Actually I think there's a lot of room, just in different places. One direction is going deep into a vertical: a specific domain where you have proprietary data, a tight feedback loop with users, and a clear notion of what "correct" means. In those settings you don't need the most general model; you need the model that's most reliable for that task, and that's often achieved through careful post-training, good evaluation, and integrating the model into a real workflow.

Another direction is efficiency and new ideas. Big companies, because they're scaling something that already works, tend to be somewhat conservative. There's a lot of organizational momentum behind the current recipe. Small teams can afford to bet on things that look strange right now: different architectures, better reasoning methods, ways to make models learn from much less data, or understanding why these models work at all. Some of my own interest is in that last part. If we understand the training dynamics better, we may find shortcuts that don't require ten times more compute. That kind of insight can come from a small group, and historically a lot of important ideas did.

And the third thing is agility. Products built around these models are changing every few months. A small company can rebuild its whole stack quickly when a new capability appears, while a large company has to coordinate many teams. So I'd say the healthy strategy for small companies is: don't fight the scaling war, ride on top of it, and focus on either a domain where you have a unique advantage, or on fundamental ideas that the big players are too busy to explore.

r001.rationale: The response says small companies should avoid competing head-on and focus on different areas, but does not characterize the two groups’ directions as initially developing in parallel.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute large companies’ convergence to senior leaders chasing the same trends.

r003.rationale: It mentions organizational momentum and coordination costs, but does not identify limited time and energy—as opposed to capability—as the constraint on researchers exploring outside the main direction.

r004.rationale: The response recommends distinct areas such as vertical applications and new ideas, and mentions small-team agility, but does not explain that pursuing different directions is specifically a way to achieve results quickly.

r005.rationale: It does not say that one small company’s demonstrated commercial success would prompt other companies to compete in that direction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the first thing to say is that small companies and large labs are not really playing the same game, and they shouldn't try to.

The large labs have one overwhelming advantage, which is compute. If your research direction is "scale the model and see what happens," then OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic will win almost by definition. A small company cannot afford to run a training job that costs hundreds of millions of dollars, fail, and run it again. So any small company whose strategy is to replicate frontier pretraining is in a very difficult position.

But I don't think scaling is the only interesting research direction, and I actually think the large labs have some structural blind spots that small teams can exploit.

The first is that frontier labs are optimizing for generality. They want one model that does everything for everyone. That's the right business goal for them, but it means a lot of problems are left on the table. If you look at a specific domain — scientific computing, hardware design, formal verification, robotics — there is often a huge gap between what a general model does and what a specialized system with the right data, the right tools, and the right inductive biases can do. A small company can go deep in one place where a large lab only goes wide.

The second is efficiency. Big labs have a lot of incentive to make models bigger, and relatively less incentive to make them small. But there is enormous demand for models that run on a laptop, on a phone, in a car, or on a single GPU in a company that doesn't want to send its data to anyone. Research on distillation, quantization, architecture search, and better inference is something a small team can do very well, because the experiments are cheap and the feedback loop is fast.

The third, and this is the one I personally find most exciting, is algorithmic and reasoning research. A lot of the recent progress in reasoning came from ideas — search, self-verification, reinforcement learning on outcomes, better use of test-time compute — not just from more parameters. Many of those ideas were tested at small scale first. A small company can invent the next one of those. You don't need ten thousand GPUs to show that a new way of training or decoding gives you a step change on a hard benchmark. Once you show it, then the big labs will adopt it, and that's fine. Being the place where the idea comes from is a real position.

The risk for small companies is the opposite failure: trying to be a worse version of a large lab. If you raise money and spend it all on a mid-size base model that's slightly behind the frontier, the frontier moves and you have nothing. The open-weight models make this even more true. If a good base model is freely available, your value has to come from what you do on top of it, not from having trained it.

So my overall view is: the large labs are converging. They are all training similar architectures on similar data with similar objectives, and the differences between them are getting smaller. That convergence actually creates room. The research directions that are not on the main scaling path — specialized domains, efficiency, new learning algorithms, agents that take real actions in the world, interpretability — those are where small companies can do work that matters, and sometimes do it better than the big players because they are forced to be creative instead of just being big.

r002.rationale: It attributes large-lab convergence to similar architectures, data, and objectives, not to senior leaders chasing the same trends.

r003.rationale: It does not identify researchers’ limited time and energy as the constraint on work outside the main direction.

r004.rationale: It describes distinct directions and notes cheap experiments and fast feedback, but does not connect pursuing those different directions to achieving results quickly.

r005.rationale: It says large labs may adopt a demonstrated idea, but does not describe commercial success triggering other companies to compete in that direction.

astra-6.text:
I think small companies need to be selective about where they compete. If the goal is to train a general-purpose model by following exactly the same approach as OpenAI, Google, or Anthropic, that’s a very difficult competition. The large companies have advantages in compute, data, infrastructure, and the number of experiments they can run.

But research progress isn’t only about scale. A small team can focus on a particular problem and move quickly. That might mean making models more efficient, improving their reliability on a specific task, or finding a better way to learn from limited data. In a specialized application, understanding the problem and having a good feedback loop can matter as much as the size of the model.

There’s also room to question assumptions. Large companies have existing systems and roadmaps to support. A small team can explore an approach that looks unconventional and hasn’t yet demonstrated that it works at scale. Of course, being different isn’t enough—you still need convincing experiments.

So I’d expect both overlap and specialization. Small companies will build on advances from the large labs, but their strongest opportunities are likely to come from identifying a bottleneck they can solve particularly well, rather than trying to reproduce the entire research agenda of a large company.

r001.rationale: The response describes overlap and specialization, but does not say the directions initially develop in parallel rather than compete directly.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute large companies’ converging research directions to senior leaders chasing the same trends.

r003.rationale: It does not identify researchers’ limited time and energy as the constraint on work outside their company’s main direction.

r004.rationale: It says small teams can focus on specific problems and move quickly, and that their best opportunities may be solving a bottleneck rather than reproducing a large company’s agenda.

r005.rationale: It does not describe demonstrated commercial success by a small company as prompting other companies to compete in that direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think small companies need to be very clear about where their advantage comes from. If you try to do exactly what OpenAI, Google, or Anthropic is doing—train a general-purpose model, but with a fraction of the compute and a much smaller team—that’s a difficult position. You may make progress, but the large companies are also moving very quickly.

That doesn’t mean all the interesting research belongs to large companies. A small team can focus on a specific problem, test ideas quickly, and pursue directions that aren’t yet a priority for a large organization. The key is to find something where a good idea and a fast feedback loop matter more than sheer scale.

For example, you might focus on a particular domain where you can evaluate whether the model actually does useful work. Then your advantage could come from understanding the task, getting the right data, and improving the whole system around the model. That can lead to research questions about reasoning, learning, or efficiency, but grounded in a concrete need.

So I wouldn’t frame it as small companies doing less ambitious research. They need a different strategy: choose a focused problem, establish an advantage, and expand from there.
